source.title: Learning from Loss Landscape: Generalizable Mixed-Precision Quantization via Adaptive Sharpness-Aware Gradient Aligning
source.authors: Lian-Bo Ma; Jian-Lun Ma; Yuee Zhou; Guo-Yang Xie; Qiang He; Zhi-Chao Lu

record.file_problem: Full paper text and supplementary material supplied.
record.tranche_reason: The study changes the sharpness-aware optimization of mixed-precision quantization and measures resulting accuracy on target datasets; its results bear conceptually on whether a sharpness measure tracks the generalization gap. It does not study ordinary unquantized networks trained on natural labels.
record.gate_note: Results concern transfer of quantization policies from proxy datasets to target datasets, including quantized model accuracy and loss sharpness. The paper does not test memorization of random labels, width scaling, architecture comparisons of convolutional versus fully connected networks, optimizer or batch-size comparisons, dropout, or removal of memorized examples. Table 1 and Table 2 compare ASGA with baseline MPQ methods; those results do not establish a result about the claim's named behaviors.
record.test_reason: The study uses a sharpness–generalization rationale to design a quantization-policy search method and reports its performance. It does not test V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure against training–test error gaps among similarly fitted networks, or compare its ranking with norm- and margin-based measures. Its other experiments test none of V1–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that ASGA searches transferable quantization policies on small proxy datasets, reduces reported sharpness, and achieves comparable or improved target performance with reduced search cost. Target evaluation follows quantization and weight fine-tuning on the target dataset; it is not transfer without target-data training.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains quantized mixed-precision policies with a sharpness-aware gradient alignment objective and evaluates transfer to target datasets; it does not use the original studies' interventions or measures of natural-label generalization gaps.
record.method_sensitivity: Perturbation radius ρ and proxy dataset affect outcomes. The paper reports that an excessively large ρ sharply reduces generalization performance, while adaptive ρ converges faster than fixed ρ without accuracy degradation. Proxy dataset selection also changes target performance; the authors attribute CIFAR10's results partly to category similarity with ImageNet.

fits_no_version.finding: ASGA reduces average reported sharpness from 13.5 to 11.4 on CIFAR10, 48.4 to 44.4 on Flowers, and 25.8 to 23.1 on Food.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: ASGA reduces the reported Hessian-based sharpness during mixed-precision quantization-policy search on the tested proxy datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: ASGA raises ImageNet Top-1 accuracy from 66.3% to 67.3% with an ImageNet-subset proxy and from 66.4% to 67.9% with a CIFAR10 proxy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: ASGA improves target accuracy for the two tested ResNet18 proxy-search settings after target-dataset fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 1 pairs lower unscaled sharpness with smaller CIFAR10-to-ImageNet accuracy differences for ALQ and EdMIPS after adding ASGA.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the illustrated quantization comparisons, lower sharpness accompanies smaller cross-dataset accuracy differences; this does not establish the magnitude-aware sharpness relationship with training–test gaps.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267 (2025)
record.problems: The study evaluates quantized models and transfer between datasets rather than standard training on natural labels or the training-test gap. Its σmax measure is not the magnitude-aware sharpness measure specified in V7. The paper does not report uncertainty estimates for the tabulated results.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 and Table 2 report many separate baseline-method accuracy and search-cost comparisons. They are omitted because they compare quantization methods and do not measure the claim's specified training-test gap or V7's stated sharpness measure. Figure 4 and Figure 6 contain additional values, including figure-only results; their fixed/adaptive-ρ and proxy-dataset comparisons are summarized in method_sensitivity and page excerpts rather than extracted as additional rows.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance performance under random labels.
Width increases beyond zero training error and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects, training-set size, underfitting, and removal with weight decay.

Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus training–test error gaps among similarly fitted networks, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. The paper's cross-dataset accuracy differences and Hessian-based sharpness are different constructs.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's use of generalization includes proxy-to-target accuracy differences, explicitly defined in Figure 1. These are not the training–test error gaps named in V7. The PAC-Bayesian bound also does not test V7's empirical ranking claim. No claim-version verdicts are warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Widening beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD generalization under tuning.
Large versus small batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets.
Effects of dropout and its removal.

The stated magnitude-aware perturbation measure and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures are not tested. The study measures loss sharpness and accuracy transfer for quantized policies across proxy and target datasets, not the training-test error gap among networks with similarly low training loss.
Removing memorized training examples and its effect on test accuracy.
